nameStory: The 'variegated' in this pond-lily's name comes from the mixed coloring on its leaves - they often show patches of green and reddish-brown that create a mottled, variegated pattern. Like other yellow pond-lilies, it gets its common name from its bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers that float on the water's surface. Some folks call it 'bullhead pond-lily' because the thick, rounded flower buds supposedly resemble a bullhead fish's blunt head.
description: Variegated yellow pond-lily is an aquatic plant that lives its entire life in the water, with thick rhizomes (underground stems) anchored in the muddy bottom. Its large, heart-shaped leaves float on the surface like green lily pads, typically 4-12 inches across, while bright yellow flowers rise just above the water on sturdy stems. This perennial plant forms colonies in quiet waters, creating patches of floating leaves that provide important habitat for frogs, turtles, and waterfowl. The whole plant can spread several feet across from a single root system.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers with 5-6 thick, waxy petals that feel leathery to the touch. The flowers smell faintly sweet and rise 1-2 inches above the water surface on thick, spongy stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, floating leaves shaped like elongated hearts with a deep notch where the stem attaches. Feel thick and rubbery, often showing reddish-brown mottling or patches mixed with green.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies of floating leaves connected by thick underwater rhizomes. Plants emerge from muddy lake or pond bottoms, with all leaves and flowers reaching the surface.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Green, bottle-shaped seed pods that feel firm and smooth, eventually splitting open to release seeds that float away. The pods often persist into fall.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, spongy underwater stems that feel hollow and flexible. When broken, they release air bubbles and have a fresh, slightly cucumber-like smell.

habitat: Found in quiet, shallow waters of ponds, slow-moving streams, and protected lake coves throughout New England. Prefers muddy or silty bottoms in water 1-6 feet deep, often growing alongside cattails, arrowhead, and pickerelweed. Thrives in slightly acidic to neutral waters and can tolerate some shade from overhanging trees.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging from the depths in late spring, unfurling at the surface as water warms. Young leaves often show more pronounced reddish coloring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, with bright yellow flowers appearing steadily. Leaves reach full size and form dense floating mats.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, while leaves may develop more variegated coloring before beginning to die back. Some leaves persist until first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: All above-water parts die back completely, leaving only the thick rhizomes buried safely in the muddy bottom, ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: The thick, spongy stems and leaf stalks are filled with air channels that work like snorkels, pumping oxygen down to the roots buried in oxygen-poor mud - you can actually hear air bubbling out if you break a stem underwater!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with white water-lilies, but those have white flowers and round leaves without the heart-shaped notch. Remember: yellow flowers and heart-shaped leaves = yellow pond-lily, white flowers and round leaves = white water-lily.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'lily,' pond-lilies aren't true lilies at all - they belong to the ancient water-lily family that's been around since before many modern plant families evolved. The 'lily' name stuck because early settlers thought the floating leaves resembled lily pads.
compareHints: Variegated yellow pond-lily differs from spatterdock by having smaller flowers and more pronounced leaf mottling, while small yellow pond-lily has much tinier leaves (usually under 4 inches) and grows in shallower water. The variegated species sits right between these two in size, making it the 'Goldilocks' of New England's yellow pond-lilies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spatterdock is the giant of New England's yellow pond-lilies, with the largest leaves and most robust growth habit.
Small yellow pond-lily is much smaller in all parts compared to spatterdock, which has leaves up to a foot across and larger, more globe-shaped flowers.
